C90B Powerplant System Overview
Understanding the powerplant… is critical for safe and efficient aircraft operation. Proper use of the engine and propeller system… extends engine life… and improves safety.
This aircraft uses the Pratt and Whitney PT6A turboprop engine… a free-turbine, reverse-flow design. In this design… the compressor and power turbine are not physically connected… allowing smoother operation and better reliability.
Air enters from the rear of the engine… moves forward through compression… combustion… and turbines… then exits at the front.
Only about 25 percent of the compressed air is used for combustion. The remaining 75 percent is used for cooling… and stabilizing the flame.
After ignition… expanding gases drive two turbine sections. The compressor turbine powers the compressor… while the power turbine drives the propeller… through a reduction gearbox.
This gearbox reduces high-speed turbine rotation… into low-speed… high-torque output for the propeller.
Engine power is measured primarily using shaft horsepower… and equivalent shaft horsepower… which includes jet thrust.
Key engine parameters include… N1… which is gas generator speed… N2… or propeller speed… ITT… interstage turbine temperature… and P3… compressor discharge pressure.
These values are critical… for both normal and emergency operations.
Fuel is delivered through a multi-stage system… including a boost pump… high-pressure pump… and fuel control unit. The fuel control unit… automatically adjusts fuel flow… to maintain the selected engine speed.
During startup… igniters provide the initial spark… but once combustion is established… the process becomes self-sustaining.
An automatic ignition system is also available… to assist in engine relight… if torque drops unexpectedly.
Lubrication is essential… for both cooling and mechanical operation. Engine oil lubricates bearings… removes heat… and powers the propeller control system.
Oil pressure and temperature must remain within limits… typically between 80 and 100 PSI… during normal operation.
The propeller system is variable-pitch… full-feathering… and reversible. Blade angle adjusts automatically… to maintain selected RPM… while optimizing thrust.
Engine power is controlled using three cockpit levers… power… propeller… and condition.
The power lever controls engine output… the propeller lever sets RPM… and the condition lever controls fuel flow… and idle speed.
As engine speed increases… torque… temperature… and fuel flow also increase.
However… engine limits must always be respected.
The two primary limits are… torque… and temperature. At low altitude or cold conditions… torque usually limits power. At high altitude or hot conditions… temperature… specifically ITT… becomes the limiting factor.
Exceeding these limits… even briefly… can damage the engine.
During engine start… ITT is especially critical. If temperature approaches the maximum limit… the start must be aborted immediately.
Oil pressure must rise quickly after start… and remain above minimum levels… to prevent damage.
Additional protections include… a compressor bleed valve… to prevent stalls at low speeds… and a chip detector… to warn of internal metal contamination.
Fuel system failures… can result in engine flameout… while boost pump failures… trigger warnings… but allow temporary operation.
Engine trend monitoring is used… to track performance over time. By recording parameters like torque… ITT… and fuel flow… pilots can detect early signs of wear… or inefficiency.
In summary… the PT6A engine is a highly reliable… and efficient turboprop system… but it requires careful monitoring… proper handling… and strict adherence to operating limits…
Mastery of these concepts… ensures safe flight operations… and maximizes engine longevity.
Propeller System Overview…
The aircraft uses constant-speed… full-feathering… reversing propellers. These propellers automatically adjust blade angle… to maintain a selected RPM.
They are driven by engine oil pressure… controlled through a propeller governor. At the same time… counterweights and springs… naturally push the blades toward feather.
This creates a balance of forces… oil pressure drives toward low pitch… while springs and counterweights drive toward high pitch… or feather.
If oil pressure is lost… the propeller will feather automatically.
Blade angle… determines thrust. Low pitch produces high RPM and thrust for takeoff… while high pitch produces lower RPM… for cruise efficiency.
The primary governor maintains constant RPM… typically between 1,800 and 2,200 RPM.
If RPM increases… an overspeed condition… the governor increases blade angle… slowing the propeller.
If RPM decreases… an underspeed condition… the governor reduces blade angle… increasing RPM.
This constant adjustment… keeps the propeller at the selected speed.
However… the system has limits.
The low pitch stop prevents the blades… from going too flat in flight. Without it… excessive drag could disrupt airflow over the tail… causing loss of control.
When the propeller reaches this stop… RPM may fall below the selected value… because the governor can no longer reduce blade angle further.
On the ground… the system allows access to Beta and reverse ranges.
In the Beta range… blade angle is directly controlled by the power lever… allowing fine thrust adjustments for taxi.
In reverse… blade angles become negative… producing reverse thrust for braking.
As reverse increases… engine power also increases… up to approximately 85 percent N1.
The power lever controls multiple things in reverse… blade angle… engine power… and propeller limits.
Improper use… such as selecting reverse when feathered… can damage the system.
The propeller can be feathered manually… by pulling the propeller lever fully aft. This removes oil pressure… allowing springs and counterweights… to align the blades with the airflow.
Feathering reduces drag… especially after engine failure.
An autofeather system is also available. When armed during takeoff… if engine torque drops… the system automatically feathers the affected propeller.
This improves aircraft control… during critical phases of flight.
Multiple backup systems protect against overspeed.
The overspeed governor… activates around 2,288 RPM… increasing blade angle to slow the propeller.
The fuel topping governor… provides an additional layer… by reducing engine power… if RPM exceeds limits.
Together… these systems prevent dangerous propeller speeds.
The cockpit includes three primary controls… power levers… propeller levers… and condition levers.
The propeller lever sets desired RPM. The power lever controls thrust… and blade angle in Beta and reverse.
A synchrophaser system improves comfort… by matching propeller RPM… and blade position… between engines.
This reduces vibration… and cabin noise.
A synchroscope indicator shows alignment… spinning left or right if propellers are out of sync… and stopping when synchronized.
In summary… the propeller system automatically balances aerodynamic forces… mechanical inputs… and pilot commands… to deliver efficient and controlled thrust.
Understanding these systems… is essential… for safe ground handling… engine-out response… and overall flight performance.
